source.title: On the Optimizer Dependence of Neural Scaling Laws

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how optimizer choice and spectral conditions affect fitted loss-scaling exponents in random-feature regression, and reports conditions where a single power-law fit becomes poor. This refines the scaling-law claim, but it is not a reproduction on language models.
record.gate_note: The study's own random-feature experiments and fit-quality results are included. Published optimizer speedups cited from other work are not rows. The proposed real-model validation is a protocol, not a result. The plotted effective-compute multiplier is parameter-equivalent, not a FLOP or wall-clock result.
record.test_reason: The study tests optimizer-dependent scaling and departures from a single power law in synthetic random-feature regression, bearing on V5 and V7. It does not test V1's language-model pretraining claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: in fixed-feature synthetic regression, preconditioning changes fitted finite-budget exponents, with the advantage generally growing with spectral steepness before saturation. The authors leave transfer to large language models and attenuation at scale unresolved. Appendix G qualifies stronger main-text language about asymptotic changes: convergence speed and finite-budget spectral allocation are not fully separated.
record.recipe_differences: Random-feature regression with fixed random features and optimizer preconditioners, rather than language-model pretraining scaling experiments. Exponents are fit by OLS over N = 200 to 5000; the study explicitly treats real-model optimizer results as qualitative context.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer type and spectral exponent change the fitted α; source exponent b changes absolute α while preserving relative optimizer ordering; input dimension D = 5000 preserves the qualitative pattern. Fit quality falls for GD and Diagonal at large s and for Sign-GD at s ≥ 0.5. The results are finite-budget dependent.
record.code_released: not stated (the paper says simulation code and analysis scripts will be made available in an anonymous repository upon publication)
record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at the 4th Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics (HiLD), ICML 2026
record.problems: The core experiments use a lazy random-feature model, not language models; only width/feature-count scaling is tested. Main experiments fix teacher source exponent b = 1.0 and use a finite training budget. GD has a large gap to the ridge optimum in some settings. Several GD and Sign-GD power-law fits are poor; Sign-GD confidence intervals are large. No direct real-model validation is run, and the authors note external evidence of optimizer-advantage attenuation at scale.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited optimizer-speedup results from Chen et al., Liu et al. and Wen et al. are excluded because they are results from other work, not this study's experiments.

untested.parts: All language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling; no language models, token scaling or compute scaling are measured.
No small-run fit is tested against held-out runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal growth law.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.

Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are untested. Evidence is confined to synthetic, fixed-feature supervised regression; the fitted size interval is 200–5000, about 1.4 decades.

No compute-optimal split, parameter-counting comparison, alternative fitting-method comparison, or explanation of disagreement between published language-model laws. Training duration is not systematically varied.

missing.what: Record the remaining Table 3 fit-quality results, especially the strong-preconditioner controls and intermediate GD/Diagonal conditions. Full NG R²: 0.999, 0.999, 0.997, 0.996, 0.992, 0.989; Matrix-Sign: 0.999, 0.999, 0.997, 0.994, 0.992, 0.993. GD at s = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0: 0.985, 0.948, 0.886, 0.806. Diagonal at those spectra: 0.987, 0.962, 0.924, 0.878. Sign-GD at s = 0.25: 0.911. Verdicts use these text-supplied results alongside the exponent rows.

The authors explicitly report that fits including N < 200 give different exponent shifts and exclude those sizes because of finite-size deviations. No numerical alternative-fit estimates are supplied.

record.verdict_notes: All exponent and diagnostic values are transcribed correctly. V1 labels should be reassigned to V5 where the power-law form is actually assessed. Finite-budget dependence supports V7 rather than limiting it. Table 3 overrides contradictory blanket fit-quality statements in Sections 3.2 and B.2. The theoretical flat-spectrum argument also contains an inconsistency: λ_i = i^{-(1+s)} approaches i^{-1}, not a constant spectrum, as s approaches zero. Published optimizer speedups and the proposed transformer protocol are not this study's experimental results.

versions.untested_parts: Tests test-loss scaling with feature count in random-feature regression only; does not test language-model pretraining, token-count scaling, or compute scaling.
No small-run fit is evaluated against the loss of a substantially larger held-out run.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token growth law is tested.
No depth, width, or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling experiment.

Tests optimizer and spectral-exponent dependence, plus fit quality over the stated model-size range. Does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, real-language-model training schedules, or fitting methods.
